note.text: A monophthong is conventionally represented as a single vowel quality, unlike a diphthong’s movement between qualities. Phonemic symbols describe a target pronunciation, not spelling letters. In the selected British dictionary model, compare /iː/ in sheep with /ɪ/ in ship, /e/ in bed with /æ/ in cat, and /ʊ/ in put with /uː/ in food. Quality matters as well as duration. English varieties differ; this page supplies written preparation, not audio assessment.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to match selected vowel symbols to model words and explain the limits of a written exercise. Builds on: Form Five sound-symbol contrasts. Leads to: oral practice and homophone distinctions.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Written model key: sheep /iː/, ship /ɪ/, bed /e/, cat /æ/, father /ɑː/, hot /ɒ/, law /ɔː/, put /ʊ/, food /uː/, cup /ʌ/, bird /ɜː/, the final vowel of sofa /ə/. The key states the chosen teaching model, not a judgement that every local accent must sound identical. Schwa is common in unstressed syllables. Ask a teacher to demonstrate and check listening and production separately.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Use the supplied model key to compare symbols and words. Do not infer a vowel sound from a letter alone. A screen choice demonstrates symbol knowledge; it does not demonstrate hearing or pronunciation. Use teacher-led listening and speaking for those skills.
